**Alexander Ulanovsky** (1891–1970) was a Soviet [resident spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident_spy "Resident spy").

## Biography

### Early spy career

In 1921, Ulanovsky was dispatched to [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") as a spy for the [Cheka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheka "Cheka"). As he had only received vague orders, he requested the Soviet embassy provide him with clearer instructions. When the embassy sent a telegraph to [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), the Cheka responded that they did not know of Ulanovsky and instructed the embassy to consider him an [agent provocateur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agent_provocateur "Agent provocateur").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202053-1) In 1927, Ulanovsky was sent to [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") as a [union representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_representative "Union representative") and met with many [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) officials under his own name.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202053%E2%80%9354-2) In October 1929, Ulanovsky and [Richard Sorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sorge "Richard Sorge") were sent to Berlin, where they made contact with [Konstantin Basov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantin_Basov?action=edit&redlink=1 "Konstantin Basov (page does not exist)"). Ulanovsky was given a fake Czech passport and the [pseudonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym") "Kirschner", under which he was to pose as a metal salesman on his way to China and offer his services as a representative to western business interests.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202054-3) His offer was taken up by the Schelder Consortium, a Dutch company seeking to circumvent the [Treaty of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles "Treaty of Versailles") so they could send German weapons to China.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202054%E2%80%9355-4) On the way to China, Ulanovsky got drunk with a group of British members of the [Shanghai Municipal Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Municipal_Police "Shanghai Municipal Police") and told them of his scheme to sell German arms to the Chinese market, jeopardising his mission.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202056-5)

### Activities in Shanghai

Upon arriving in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai") in January 1930, Ulanovsky and Sorge made contact with Soviet agent [Alexander Gurvich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gurvich "Alexander Gurvich").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202059-6) Ulanovsky had been instructed to form an entirely new network of agents, as Gurvich's had been compromised, causing conflict between him and Gurvich, who had not been informed of the change in advance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202059%E2%80%9360-7) After a fortnight in Shanghai, Ulanovsky reported that Sorge had managed to ingratiate himself in the German quarter of the [Shanghai International Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_International_Settlement "Shanghai International Settlement") and that they had discovered a conflict between [Chiang Kai-Shek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-Shek "Chiang Kai-Shek") and the German colonisers, who opposed his [nationalisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalisation "Nationalisation") policies. Ulanovsky and Sorge also joined a local Christian youth organisation, but they were not able to discover anything through this.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202061-8) One night, Ulanovsky was recognised by a German businessman, who had attended one of his 1927 speeches where he had acted under his own name as a union representative. This forced him to avoid the German community and jeopardised his cover identity, effectively rendering him unable to act.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202073%E2%80%9374-9)

In the spring of 1930, Ulanovsky recruited the agent [Rafail Kurgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafail_Kurgan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rafail Kurgan (page does not exist)"), who managed to bribe a secretary in the [Nationalist government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_government "Nationalist government") to hand over information on audits of Chinese generals and contracts with western companies. Following this success, Kurgan asked Ulanovsky for more money and then disappeared with it for almost a month. On 12 June 1930, he returned to Ulanovsky and again asked him for money; as Kurgan knew Ulanovsky and his wife's real names and addresses, Ulanovsky handed the money over. He initially attempted to explain the lost money as Kurgan's gambling losses, but on 16 July 1930, he admitted to the Soviet bureau that he was being blackmailed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202076-10) The following month, Kurgan again demanded money from Ulanovsky; he and his wife paid for a train ticket to [Harbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbin "Harbin") and Kurgan again disappeared. Ulanovsky was later told by the Soviet double agent [Evgeny Kozhevnikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evgeny_Kozhevnikov?action=edit&redlink=1 "Evgeny Kozhevnikov (page does not exist)") that Kurgan had stayed in Shanghai and that he had been arrested for forgery. When Kozhevnikov requested money from Ulanovsky to help get Kurgan out of jail, Ulanovsky threw him out of his house. Realising that they could not remain under cover in Shanghai, Ulanovsky recommended Sorge replace him as head of the Shanghai bureau and, together with his wife, fled to [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") by boat.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202077-11)

### Activities in the United States

In 1931, Ulanovsky arrived in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where he replaced [Moishe Stern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Stern "Manfred Stern") as [station chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Station_chief "Station chief") of the local branch of the [Main Intelligence Directorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)") (GRU).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy20186-12) From this position, throughout the 1930s, Ulanovsky worked as the [handler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agent_handling "Agent handling") of the American communist defectors Whittaker Chambers,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews202054Murphy20186Murphy201986Znamenski2017341-13)[Leon Muenster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Muenster?action=edit&redlink=1 "Leon Muenster (page does not exist)"), [Robert Osman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Osman?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robert Osman (page does not exist)"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy20186-12)[Lydia Stahl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Stahl "Lydia Stahl"), [Robert Gordon Switz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gordon_Switz "Robert Gordon Switz"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy20186Murphy201986-14)[Marjorie Tilley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_Tilley?action=edit&redlink=1 "Marjorie Tilley (page does not exist)")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy201986-15) and [Joshua Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Turner_(spy)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Joshua Turner (spy) (page does not exist)").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy20186-12) Chambers worked for Ulanovsky until 1938, when he received news of the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge") and went into hiding.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy201996-16) Chambers later wrote extensively about Ulanovsky in his autobiography.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurphy201998n55-17) Following his return to the Soviet Union, Ulanovsky was incarcerated in a [Gulag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag "Gulag"), where he read many history books, particularly taking interest in the [Khazar Khaganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khazar_Khaganate "Khazar Khaganate"). He was released in 1954, following the [death of Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Joseph_Stalin "Death of Joseph Stalin").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alexander_Ulanovsky&printable=yes#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZnamenski2017341-18)

**Nadezhda (Esther) Markovna Ulanovskaya** (1903–1986), nicknamed **Nadia** or **Nadya**, was a Soviet intelligence [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)") officer, translator, English teacher, wife of Alexander Ulanovsky, and mother of [Maya Ulanovskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Ulanovskaya "Maya Ulanovskaya").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Family2016-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-OpenList-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Bereszada.jpg/250px-Bereszada.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bereszada.jpg)

Former Moszyński Palace in [Bershad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bershad "Bershad"), Ulanovskaya's birthplace

Nadezhda Ulanovskaya was born Esther Markovna Fridgant in [Bershad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bershad "Bershad") in the then [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") (now [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine")). Her father was a trader; her grandfather Nukhim Fridgant was a rabbi and possibly a descendant of a Hasidic tzaddik Reful (Friedgant). Ulanovskaya studied in private and village schools. In 1917, after the [February Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution "February Revolution"), the family moved to [Odessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odessa "Odessa").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Family2016-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-OpenList-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/19170704_Riot_on_Nevsky_prosp_Petrograd.jpg/250px-19170704_Riot_on_Nevsky_prosp_Petrograd.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:19170704_Riot_on_Nevsky_prosp_Petrograd.jpg)

Ulanovskaya supported the [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution") (here, [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg") on 4 July 1917 during demonstration on [Nevsky Prospekt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevsky_Prospekt "Nevsky Prospekt") following machine gunning by troops of [Provisional Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Provisional_Government "Russian Provisional Government"))

After the 1917 [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution"), Ulanovskaya joined the Young Revolutionary International as an anarchist and changed her name from Esther to _Nadezhda_ ("Hope"). During the [Russian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Civil_War "Russian Civil War"), she worked for the pro-Soviet underground in Odessa by distributing leaflets. At this time, she met her future husband, Alexander Ulanovsky. In April 1919, during the flight of [White Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_movement "White movement") from Odessa, she helped occupy the Odessa police station. In August 1919, ahead of the White Russian re-occupation of Odessa, she evacuated with Ulanovsky to Nikolaev ([Mykolaiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mykolaiv "Mykolaiv") in Ukraine) and eventually returned to Odessa. In 1921, she and Ulanovsky visited Germany on behalf of the [Cheka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheka "Cheka"). In 1922, they moved to Moscow.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

### Communism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Communism")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-1985-1003-020%2C_Richard_Sorge.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-1985-1003-020%2C_Richard_Sorge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-1985-1003-020,_Richard_Sorge.jpg)

In 1928, Ulanovskaya was stationed by the [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)") with her husband and [Richard Sorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sorge "Richard Sorge") (here in 1940)

In 1923, under the name of "Maria Andreyevna Sorokina," Ulanovskaya worked with her husband in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg") for the [Profintern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profintern "Profintern"), after which the Ulanovskys returned to Moscow (still with the Profintern).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In 1928, the Ulanovskys joined the Soviet military intelligence service (or [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Intelligence_Directorate_(GRU) "Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU)")). With [Richard Sorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sorge "Richard Sorge"), they were stationed in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2) In 1929, she went with her husband to China as a lieutenant for "technical work."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) Her job there was radio operator under the name of a [Sudeten German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudeten_German "Sudeten German") "Kirschner."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2) In 1930, the Ulanovskys were expelled from Shanghai.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

In 1930–1931, the Ulanovskys lived in Berlin and Paris. In 1931, they traveled to the United States as Canadians named "Goldman" and then operated in the US under the surname "Zhuratovich."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2) While stationed in New York 1932–4 as employees of [AMTORG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtorg_Trading_Corporation "Amtorg Trading Corporation"), one of the agents in their spy network was Whittaker Chambers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) While stationed in the US, Ulanovskaya met her uncle, who had immigrated to the US in 1913.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

At some point 1933–1935, the Ulanovskys were stationed in Denmark to support Soviet espionage in Germany (after [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s takeover in early 1933 and uprooting of Soviet intelligence in Germany). Her husband was caught and imprisoned in a public spy scandal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

In 1932 (or 1934?), Ulanovskaya returned to Moscow, where, still in Soviet military intelligence, she studied at the [Institute of Foreign Languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_Linguistic_University "Moscow State Linguistic University") through 1941. She also worked as an English teacher at the Frunze Military Academy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

During the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge"), the Ulanovskys "broke with the party." Ulanovsky had to leave the Fourth Section of the Red Army (Intelligence, aka [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)")).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

During World War II, Ulanovsky fought in the war, during which he was demoted to captain and wounded; Ulanovskaya sent her children East with her mother to [Chelyabinsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelyabinsk "Chelyabinsk") for safety.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) She worked with foreign correspondents with the Commissariat of Foreign Affairs, including work in the Far East. In 1947, she taught English at the [Institute of International Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_Institute_of_International_Relations "Moscow State Institute of International Relations"); in December 1947, she was dismissed due to pending arrest.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

### GULAG

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: GULAG")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Dubravlag-map.png/250px-Dubravlag-map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dubravlag-map.png)

[Dubravlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubravlag "Dubravlag"), where Ulanovskaya served prison time

On 21 February 1948, Ulanovskaya was arrested for treason, specifically the transfer of information about the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge") for Australian [Godfrey Blunden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_Blunden "Godfrey Blunden") for the 1947 book _A Room on the Route_ published in the US. She was locked in solitary confinement in the [Lefortovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefortovo_Prison "Lefortovo Prison") prison. (Her husband was arrested on 3 March 1949.)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) Accused of working with a British and American spy, she was not allowed to sleep for 13 days and nights.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

In 1951, she received a 15-year sentence in labor camps. She served time in [Rechlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rechlag "Rechlag") and then [Dubravlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubravlag "Dubravlag"). (In 1951, her daughter was also arrested and in 1952 sentenced to 25 years.) In May 1956, Soviet authorities reclassified her crime to "disclosure of official secrets," reduced the sentence to the time already served, and released her.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-OpenList-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

### Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later years")]

In 1961, her younger daughter died. In 1971, her husband died.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In 1973, Ulanovskaya immigrated to Israel with her daughter Maya, son-in-law, and grandson.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In 1977, mother and daughter visited Godfrey Blunden in Europe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In July 1977, [C. L. Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger "C. L. Sulzberger") of the _New York Times_ visited Ulanovskaya in Israel and published some recollections of her from his days in Moscow as bureau chief 1943–5.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

On 26 July 1977, in London, Ulanovskaya appeared on an episode called "The Soviet Intelligence Apparatus" on _[Firing Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing\_Line\_(TV\_series) "Firing Line (TV series)")_, a talk show hosted by [William F. Buckley Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_F._Buckley_Jr. "William F. Buckley Jr."):[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-FiringLine-5)

> **Ulanovskaya:** When we were in the States [in the Thirties], it was the first time—not that I began to doubt, but that I felt, with some reason, we couldn't do what the capitalists had achieved... In the States, in spite of that terrible time of the [Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression")... to us it didn't look terrible at all.   
> **Buckley:** You mean by contrast with what you had experienced?   
> **Ulanovskaya:** We saw those jobless people who still ate better... You know, some Communist sympathizers once showed us some slums, but those slums didn't impress me at all.  
> **Buckley:** Made you feel at home?   
> **Ulanovskaya:** Well, the way we personally lived in Moscow at that time was worse.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-FiringLine-5)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/71/My_Father%282%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:My_Father(2).jpg)

Ulanovskaya married [Alexander Petrovich Ulanovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Petrovich_Ulanovsky "Alexander Petrovich Ulanovsky"), fellow Soviet spy

By 1922, Ulanovskaya had married Alexander Ulanovsky. They had a son and two daughters, of whom one is named [Maya Ulanovskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Ulanovskaya "Maya Ulanovskaya").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

According to Sulzberger's 1977 memoir, Ulanovskaya had never heard of [Alger Hiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alger_Hiss "Alger Hiss"), and her husband had no contact with [Kim Philby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Philby "Kim Philby"), [Guy Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Burgess "Guy Burgess"), or [Donald McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Maclean_(spy) "Donald Maclean (spy)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

On 5 January 1986, Nadezhda Ulanovskaya died in Israel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

**Nadezhda (Esther) Markovna Ulanovskaya** (1903–1986), nicknamed **Nadia** or **Nadya**, was a Soviet intelligence [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)") officer, translator, English teacher, wife of Alexander Ulanovsky, and mother of [Maya Ulanovskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Ulanovskaya "Maya Ulanovskaya").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Family2016-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-OpenList-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Bereszada.jpg/250px-Bereszada.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bereszada.jpg)

Former Moszyński Palace in [Bershad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bershad "Bershad"), Ulanovskaya's birthplace

Nadezhda Ulanovskaya was born Esther Markovna Fridgant in [Bershad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bershad "Bershad") in the then [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") (now [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine")). Her father was a trader; her grandfather Nukhim Fridgant was a rabbi and possibly a descendant of a Hasidic tzaddik Reful (Friedgant). Ulanovskaya studied in private and village schools. In 1917, after the [February Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution "February Revolution"), the family moved to [Odessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odessa "Odessa").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Family2016-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-OpenList-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/19170704_Riot_on_Nevsky_prosp_Petrograd.jpg/250px-19170704_Riot_on_Nevsky_prosp_Petrograd.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:19170704_Riot_on_Nevsky_prosp_Petrograd.jpg)

Ulanovskaya supported the [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution") (here, [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg") on 4 July 1917 during demonstration on [Nevsky Prospekt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevsky_Prospekt "Nevsky Prospekt") following machine gunning by troops of [Provisional Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Provisional_Government "Russian Provisional Government"))

After the 1917 [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution"), Ulanovskaya joined the Young Revolutionary International as an anarchist and changed her name from Esther to _Nadezhda_ ("Hope"). During the [Russian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Civil_War "Russian Civil War"), she worked for the pro-Soviet underground in Odessa by distributing leaflets. At this time, she met her future husband, Alexander Ulanovsky. In April 1919, during the flight of [White Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_movement "White movement") from Odessa, she helped occupy the Odessa police station. In August 1919, ahead of the White Russian re-occupation of Odessa, she evacuated with Ulanovsky to Nikolaev ([Mykolaiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mykolaiv "Mykolaiv") in Ukraine) and eventually returned to Odessa. In 1921, she and Ulanovsky visited Germany on behalf of the [Cheka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheka "Cheka"). In 1922, they moved to Moscow.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

### Communism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Communism")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-1985-1003-020%2C_Richard_Sorge.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-1985-1003-020%2C_Richard_Sorge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-1985-1003-020,_Richard_Sorge.jpg)

In 1928, Ulanovskaya was stationed by the [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)") with her husband and [Richard Sorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sorge "Richard Sorge") (here in 1940)

In 1923, under the name of "Maria Andreyevna Sorokina," Ulanovskaya worked with her husband in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg") for the [Profintern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profintern "Profintern"), after which the Ulanovskys returned to Moscow (still with the Profintern).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In 1928, the Ulanovskys joined the Soviet military intelligence service (or [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Intelligence_Directorate_(GRU) "Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU)")). With [Richard Sorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sorge "Richard Sorge"), they were stationed in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2) In 1929, she went with her husband to China as a lieutenant for "technical work."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) Her job there was radio operator under the name of a [Sudeten German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudeten_German "Sudeten German") "Kirschner."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2) In 1930, the Ulanovskys were expelled from Shanghai.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

In 1930–1931, the Ulanovskys lived in Berlin and Paris. In 1931, they traveled to the United States as Canadians named "Goldman" and then operated in the US under the surname "Zhuratovich."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2) While stationed in New York 1932–4 as employees of [AMTORG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtorg_Trading_Corporation "Amtorg Trading Corporation"), one of the agents in their spy network was Whittaker Chambers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) While stationed in the US, Ulanovskaya met her uncle, who had immigrated to the US in 1913.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

At some point 1933–1935, the Ulanovskys were stationed in Denmark to support Soviet espionage in Germany (after [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s takeover in early 1933 and uprooting of Soviet intelligence in Germany). Her husband was caught and imprisoned in a public spy scandal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

In 1932 (or 1934?), Ulanovskaya returned to Moscow, where, still in Soviet military intelligence, she studied at the [Institute of Foreign Languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_Linguistic_University "Moscow State Linguistic University") through 1941. She also worked as an English teacher at the Frunze Military Academy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

During the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge"), the Ulanovskys "broke with the party." Ulanovsky had to leave the Fourth Section of the Red Army (Intelligence, aka [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(Soviet_Union) "GRU (Soviet Union)")).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

During World War II, Ulanovsky fought in the war, during which he was demoted to captain and wounded; Ulanovskaya sent her children East with her mother to [Chelyabinsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelyabinsk "Chelyabinsk") for safety.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) She worked with foreign correspondents with the Commissariat of Foreign Affairs, including work in the Far East. In 1947, she taught English at the [Institute of International Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_Institute_of_International_Relations "Moscow State Institute of International Relations"); in December 1947, she was dismissed due to pending arrest.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

### GULAG

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: GULAG")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Dubravlag-map.png/250px-Dubravlag-map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dubravlag-map.png)

[Dubravlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubravlag "Dubravlag"), where Ulanovskaya served prison time

On 21 February 1948, Ulanovskaya was arrested for treason, specifically the transfer of information about the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge") for Australian [Godfrey Blunden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_Blunden "Godfrey Blunden") for the 1947 book _A Room on the Route_ published in the US. She was locked in solitary confinement in the [Lefortovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefortovo_Prison "Lefortovo Prison") prison. (Her husband was arrested on 3 March 1949.)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4) Accused of working with a British and American spy, she was not allowed to sleep for 13 days and nights.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

In 1951, she received a 15-year sentence in labor camps. She served time in [Rechlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rechlag "Rechlag") and then [Dubravlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubravlag "Dubravlag"). (In 1951, her daughter was also arrested and in 1952 sentenced to 25 years.) In May 1956, Soviet authorities reclassified her crime to "disclosure of official secrets," reduced the sentence to the time already served, and released her.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-OpenList-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

### Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later years")]

In 1961, her younger daughter died. In 1971, her husband died.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In 1973, Ulanovskaya immigrated to Israel with her daughter Maya, son-in-law, and grandson.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In 1977, mother and daughter visited Godfrey Blunden in Europe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

In July 1977, [C. L. Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger "C. L. Sulzberger") of the _New York Times_ visited Ulanovskaya in Israel and published some recollections of her from his days in Moscow as bureau chief 1943–5.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

On 26 July 1977, in London, Ulanovskaya appeared on an episode called "The Soviet Intelligence Apparatus" on _[Firing Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing\_Line\_(TV\_series) "Firing Line (TV series)")_, a talk show hosted by [William F. Buckley Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_F._Buckley_Jr. "William F. Buckley Jr."):[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-FiringLine-5)

> **Ulanovskaya:** When we were in the States [in the Thirties], it was the first time—not that I began to doubt, but that I felt, with some reason, we couldn't do what the capitalists had achieved... In the States, in spite of that terrible time of the [Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression")... to us it didn't look terrible at all.   
> **Buckley:** You mean by contrast with what you had experienced?   
> **Ulanovskaya:** We saw those jobless people who still ate better... You know, some Communist sympathizers once showed us some slums, but those slums didn't impress me at all.  
> **Buckley:** Made you feel at home?   
> **Ulanovskaya:** Well, the way we personally lived in Moscow at that time was worse.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-FiringLine-5)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/71/My_Father%282%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:My_Father(2).jpg)

Ulanovskaya married [Alexander Petrovich Ulanovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Petrovich_Ulanovsky "Alexander Petrovich Ulanovsky"), fellow Soviet spy

By 1922, Ulanovskaya had married Alexander Ulanovsky. They had a son and two daughters, of whom one is named [Maya Ulanovskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Ulanovskaya "Maya Ulanovskaya").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

According to Sulzberger's 1977 memoir, Ulanovskaya had never heard of [Alger Hiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alger_Hiss "Alger Hiss"), and her husband had no contact with [Kim Philby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Philby "Kim Philby"), [Guy Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Burgess "Guy Burgess"), or [Donald McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Maclean_(spy) "Donald Maclean (spy)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Hen-4)

On 5 January 1986, Nadezhda Ulanovskaya died in Israel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Ulanovskaya#cite_note-Sakharov-2)

**Cyrus Leo Sulzberger II** (October 27, 1912 – September 20, 1993) was an American journalist, diarist, and non-fiction writer. He was a member of the family that owned _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ and he was that newspaper's lead [foreign correspondent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_correspondent "Foreign correspondent") during the 1940s and 1950s.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C._L._Sulzberger&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Sulzberger was born in New York City on October 27, 1912 to Leopold Sulzberger (1885–1926) and Beatrice A Josephi (1890-?). He was the grandson of [Cyrus Leopold Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Leopold_Sulzberger "Cyrus Leopold Sulzberger") and the nephew of [Arthur Hays Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Hays_Sulzberger "Arthur Hays Sulzberger"), who was publisher of _The New York Times_ from 1935 to 1961.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-NYT-2) He graduated _[magna cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna\_cum\_laude "Magna cum laude")_ from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in 1934. Cy, as he was commonly called, joined the family paper in 1939 and was soon covering stories oversea as Europe edged toward [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Among the reporters who worked for him during the war were [Drew Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drew_Middleton?action=edit&redlink=1 "Drew Middleton (page does not exist)") and [James Reston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Reston "James Reston"). He served as a foreign affairs correspondent for 40 years and wrote two dozen books in his lifetime.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-NYT-2) His skills as a raconteur were legendary as were his friendships with high and mighty or just plain interesting people. Because of the circles he traveled in, he sometimes carried messages from one foreign leader to another; for U.S. President [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") he conveyed a note to Soviet premier [Nikita Khrushchev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev") in 1961. Of all the leaders he befriended, it is said that he was closest to President [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle "Charles de Gaulle") of France.

In a 1977 article for _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, journalist [Carl Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Bernstein "Carl Bernstein") included Sulzberger in a group of columnists and commentators whose [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") relationships Bernstein characterized as going "far beyond those normally maintained between reporters and their sources." He cited CIA files as referring to Sulzberger as what the agency called "known assets." Bernstein quoted unnamed CIA officials as saying Sulzberger at one time published a briefing paper the CIA provided him almost verbatim under his byline. Bernstein then quoted Sulzberger as calling that allegation "a lot of baloney" and insisting that while the agency might have considered him "an asset," in the sense of his willingness to answer questions about his travels to (fictitious nations) "[Slobovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slobovia "Slobovia")" or "[Ruritania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruritania "Ruritania")," he never took formal assignments from the agency nor would "get caught near the spook business."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-cia-3) The Times also denied that Sulzberger had ever been a paid CIA agent.

Sulzberger received a [Pulitzer Prize Special Citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards") in 1951 for his "exclusive interview" with imprisoned [Archbishop of Zagreb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Zagreb "Archbishop of Zagreb")[Aloysius Stepinac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aloysius_Stepinac "Aloysius Stepinac").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-pulitzer-4)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C._L._Sulzberger&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 1942 Sulzberger married Marina Tatiana Ladas, a [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_people "Greek people") who was often his travel companion and ensured that they had an active and elegant social life in Paris. She died in 1976 and he died at their Paris home on September 20, 1993.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-LAT-5) They had two children: David Alexis Sulzberger and Marina Beatrice Sulzberger.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-NYT-2) In 1967, Marina Beatrice Sulzberger married [Adrian Michael Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Berry,_4th_Viscount_Camrose "Adrian Berry, 4th Viscount Camrose"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-6) who later became 4th Viscount Camrose, thereby linking two newspaper dynasties. The Camrose family had once owned _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ and retained an interest in that paper until it was taken over by [Conrad Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_Black "Conrad Black") in 1986.

## Selected books

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C._L._Sulzberger&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Selected books")]

*   _Sit Down with John L. Lewis_ (New York: Random House, 1938) — about CIO founder [John L. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_L._Lewis "John L. Lewis")
*   _The American Heritage Picture History of World War II_ (New York: American Heritage, 1966), by Sulzberger with the editors of _[American Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Heritage\_(magazine) "American Heritage (magazine)")_
*   _A Long Row of Candles: Memoirs and Diaries, 1934-1954_ (New York: Macmillan, 1969)
*   _The Tooth Merchant: A Novel_ (New York: Quadrangle, 1973) — a novel in which Sulzberger himself appears briefly as a journalist
*   _An Age of Mediocrity: Memoirs and Diaries, 1963-1972_ (New York: Macmillan, 1973)
*   _Go Gentle Into the Night_ (Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall, Inc., 1976) – Sulzberger's anthology of prayers
*   _The Fall of Eagles_ (New York: Crown Publishers, 1977)

**Cyrus Leo Sulzberger II** (October 27, 1912 – September 20, 1993) was an American journalist, diarist, and non-fiction writer. He was a member of the family that owned _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ and he was that newspaper's lead [foreign correspondent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_correspondent "Foreign correspondent") during the 1940s and 1950s.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C._L._Sulzberger&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Sulzberger was born in New York City on October 27, 1912 to Leopold Sulzberger (1885–1926) and Beatrice A Josephi (1890-?). He was the grandson of [Cyrus Leopold Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Leopold_Sulzberger "Cyrus Leopold Sulzberger") and the nephew of [Arthur Hays Sulzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Hays_Sulzberger "Arthur Hays Sulzberger"), who was publisher of _The New York Times_ from 1935 to 1961.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-NYT-2) He graduated _[magna cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna\_cum\_laude "Magna cum laude")_ from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in 1934. Cy, as he was commonly called, joined the family paper in 1939 and was soon covering stories oversea as Europe edged toward [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Among the reporters who worked for him during the war were [Drew Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drew_Middleton?action=edit&redlink=1 "Drew Middleton (page does not exist)") and [James Reston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Reston "James Reston"). He served as a foreign affairs correspondent for 40 years and wrote two dozen books in his lifetime.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-NYT-2) His skills as a raconteur were legendary as were his friendships with high and mighty or just plain interesting people. Because of the circles he traveled in, he sometimes carried messages from one foreign leader to another; for U.S. President [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") he conveyed a note to Soviet premier [Nikita Khrushchev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev") in 1961. Of all the leaders he befriended, it is said that he was closest to President [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle "Charles de Gaulle") of France.

In a 1977 article for _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, journalist [Carl Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Bernstein "Carl Bernstein") included Sulzberger in a group of columnists and commentators whose [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") relationships Bernstein characterized as going "far beyond those normally maintained between reporters and their sources." He cited CIA files as referring to Sulzberger as what the agency called "known assets." Bernstein quoted unnamed CIA officials as saying Sulzberger at one time published a briefing paper the CIA provided him almost verbatim under his byline. Bernstein then quoted Sulzberger as calling that allegation "a lot of baloney" and insisting that while the agency might have considered him "an asset," in the sense of his willingness to answer questions about his travels to (fictitious nations) "[Slobovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slobovia "Slobovia")" or "[Ruritania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruritania "Ruritania")," he never took formal assignments from the agency nor would "get caught near the spook business."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-cia-3) The Times also denied that Sulzberger had ever been a paid CIA agent.

Sulzberger received a [Pulitzer Prize Special Citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards") in 1951 for his "exclusive interview" with imprisoned [Archbishop of Zagreb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Zagreb "Archbishop of Zagreb")[Aloysius Stepinac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aloysius_Stepinac "Aloysius Stepinac").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-pulitzer-4)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C._L._Sulzberger&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 1942 Sulzberger married Marina Tatiana Ladas, a [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_people "Greek people") who was often his travel companion and ensured that they had an active and elegant social life in Paris. She died in 1976 and he died at their Paris home on September 20, 1993.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-LAT-5) They had two children: David Alexis Sulzberger and Marina Beatrice Sulzberger.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-NYT-2) In 1967, Marina Beatrice Sulzberger married [Adrian Michael Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Berry,_4th_Viscount_Camrose "Adrian Berry, 4th Viscount Camrose"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._L._Sulzberger#cite_note-6) who later became 4th Viscount Camrose, thereby linking two newspaper dynasties. The Camrose family had once owned _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ and retained an interest in that paper until it was taken over by [Conrad Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_Black "Conrad Black") in 1986.

## Selected books

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C._L._Sulzberger&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Selected books")]

*   _Sit Down with John L. Lewis_ (New York: Random House, 1938) — about CIO founder [John L. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_L._Lewis "John L. Lewis")
*   _The American Heritage Picture History of World War II_ (New York: American Heritage, 1966), by Sulzberger with the editors of _[American Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Heritage\_(magazine) "American Heritage (magazine)")_
*   _A Long Row of Candles: Memoirs and Diaries, 1934-1954_ (New York: Macmillan, 1969)
*   _The Tooth Merchant: A Novel_ (New York: Quadrangle, 1973) — a novel in which Sulzberger himself appears briefly as a journalist
*   _An Age of Mediocrity: Memoirs and Diaries, 1963-1972_ (New York: Macmillan, 1973)
*   _Go Gentle Into the Night_ (Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall, Inc., 1976) – Sulzberger's anthology of prayers
*   _The Fall of Eagles_ (New York: Crown Publishers, 1977)
